metadata.name: bedrock-agentcore
metadata.overview:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating AI agents at scale. It works with popular open-source agent frameworks and with foundation models hosted in or outside Amazon Bedrock. It helps teams avoid building and managing specialized agent infrastructure.

Agents run in isolated, managed sessions that can support real-time interactions and long-running tasks. The platform helps agents retain short-term and long-term context, and it connects agents to existing APIs, functions, and services as tools. It also lets agents execute code in sandboxes and interact with websites through a managed browser.

Built-in identity and credential management helps agents authenticate users and access third-party services with scoped permissions. Deterministic policy controls, tracing, monitoring, and quality evaluation help teams govern agent behavior and improve performance in production.
useCases: Deploying production customer-support, workflow-automation, data-analysis, or coding-assistant agents built with open-source frameworks onto managed infrastructure where each user session runs in its own isolated environment with persistent conversational memory.

Turning existing internal APIs, serverless functions, OpenAPI-described services, and workflow state machines into governed tools that any MCP-compatible agent can discover and call through a single entry point with centralized inbound and outbound authentication.

Building an internal agent platform that gives developer teams a paved path with approved tools, shared memory stores, deterministic policy guardrails on tool calls, and centralized monitoring and auditing across accounts.

Allowing agents to act on behalf of end users in third-party SaaS applications such as Slack, GitHub, Google Drive, or Salesforce using user-consented delegated access, with credentials held in a managed vault rather than embedded in agent code.

Running untrusted, AI-generated code for data analysis and automating web tasks such as navigation, form filling, and information extraction inside sandboxed interpreters and managed browsers, with session recording available for review and audit.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Control-plane counterpart that shares the bedrock-agentcore IAM prefix; creates and manages the runtimes, endpoints, memories, gateways, browsers, code interpreters, workload identities, credential providers, payment managers, policy engines, evaluators and harnesses that this data-plane namespace invokes. CloudFormation AWS::BedrockAgentCore types are provisioned through its Create operations.

Foundation models invoked by agents, harnesses, memory extraction strategies and evaluators; Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied through Policy in AgentCore and to screen memory prompts; Bedrock managed knowledge bases available as gateway connector targets.
Model inference API (InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream) called by agent execution roles and gateway inference targets.
Existing Agents for Amazon Bedrock can be translated into AgentCore Runtime code by the AgentCore CLI; Bedrock managed knowledge bases can be exposed as gateway connector targets.

AWS Agent Registry data plane is migrating out of the bedrock-agentcore namespace (legacy SearchRegistryRecords) into the dedicated agent-registry namespace; the old namespace shuts down for registry on October 30, 2026.
Control plane for AWS Agent Registry registries and records after migration; owns the AWS::AgentRegistry CloudFormation types (excluded from this namespace's CFN prefixes).
Lambda functions serve as AgentCore Gateway MCP targets and as request/response interceptors that run custom authentication or authorization logic.
Amazon API Gateway stages can be added as AgentCore Gateway targets (IAM, API key or no outbound authorization).
AWS Step Functions built-in connector target exposes state machine operations as MCP tools; harnesses can be invoked from Step Functions via an InvokeHarness state.
Encrypts data at rest with AWS owned keys by default; customer managed keys supported for memories, gateways, token vaults, policy engines, batch evaluations, recommendations and other resources.

Stores credential provider secrets for AgentCore Identity (OAuth client secrets, API keys, payment credentials), browser proxy basic-auth credentials and custom root CA certificates for browser and code interpreter sessions.

Service storage of data at rest; customer buckets for browser session recordings, browser extensions and enterprise policies, harness skills, direct code deployment artifacts, self-managed memory payload delivery, and CloudTrail data-event logs.
Amazon S3 Files access points can be mounted into runtime, browser and code interpreter sessions as file systems.
Amazon EFS access points can be mounted over NFS into runtime, browser and code interpreter sessions (bring-your-own file systems).
Container images for agent runtimes are pulled from Amazon ECR; ECR VPC endpoints are required for VPC-mode runtimes without internet access.
The AgentCore CLI uses AWS CodeBuild to build container images during deployment.
AgentCore CLI deploys projects with AWS CDK and CloudFormation stacks; AgentCore resources are modeled as AWS::BedrockAgentCore resource types.
AgentCore built-in metrics, observability dashboards, WAF metrics and evaluation result metrics are published to Amazon CloudWatch.
Runtime and tool logs, executed-command audit logs, vended payments logs, and batch evaluation/recommendation trace sources and result destinations use CloudWatch Logs.
Agent traces and spans (including payment lifecycle spans) are sent to AWS X-Ray; the CLI enables CloudWatch Transaction Search.
AgentCore deploy enables CloudWatch Transaction Search/Application Signals discovery; BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess grants application-signals permissions.
CloudWatch Observability Access Manager sinks and links enable cross-account monitoring of AgentCore resources.
AWS Organizations is the recommended way to link source accounts for cross-account AgentCore observability (aws:PrincipalOrgID-scoped sink policies).
Records AgentCore management events and opt-in data events (e.g., InvokeAgentRuntime, InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand, InvokeGateway) for auditing.
VPC mode creates ENIs in customer subnets via a service-linked role; Runtime Instances run on EC2 managed instances in the customer account; interface VPC endpoints provide private connectivity.
Gateway VPC egress to private targets and private (VPC-hosted) identity providers use Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateways managed through service-linked roles.
Regional AWS WAF web ACLs can be associated with AgentCore gateways to inspect inbound requests.
Identity-based and resource-based policies, service-specific condition keys, execution/service roles and service-linked roles govern AgentCore access.
AgentCore assumes customer execution roles via sts:AssumeRole trust policies (protected with aws:SourceArn/aws:SourceAccount).
Self-managed memory strategies publish job notifications to Amazon SNS topics (including cross-account topics).
Memory record streaming publishes memory record lifecycle events to customer Kinesis Data Streams.
Kinesis Video Streams managed TURN relays WebRTC media between clients and agents on AgentCore Runtime.
Amazon Cognito user pools are a supported identity provider for inbound JWT authorization of runtimes and gateways.
AgentCore stores data at rest (including gateway customer data and metadata) in Amazon DynamoDB.
AgentCore Gateway integrates with AWS Certificate Manager (e.g., for custom domain names).
Registry record and registry lifecycle notifications are emitted to the default EventBridge bus (legacy source aws.bedrock-agentcore, migrating to aws.agent-registry).

entities.name: AbTest
entities.overview:
An A/B test in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore compares two versions of an agent using live production traffic. It routes incoming sessions to a control or treatment variant through an AgentCore Gateway, without changes to agent code.

Each variant references either a gateway target, such as a separate runtime endpoint, or a configuration bundle version on a shared runtime. Session assignment is sticky, so each conversation stays on one variant. Online evaluation scores completed sessions, and the service reports per-evaluator statistics, including confidence intervals and significance.

A/B tests help teams validate prompt, model, tool-description, or code changes on real traffic before a full rollout. Tests can be started, paused, resumed, or stopped, and stopping returns traffic to the default routing.

entities.name: AgentRuntime
entities.overview:
An agent runtime hosts AI agent or tool code in a secure, serverless environment built for agentic workloads. It works with any agent framework or foundation model. It also supports common agent communication protocols such as MCP and A2A.

Each user session runs in a dedicated, isolated execution environment with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem. Context carries across interactions within a session and is cleared when the session ends. This helps keep one user's data out of another user's session.

The runtime supports streaming and long-running interactions, deterministic shell commands within a session, and private connectivity to resources in your VPC. Built-in inbound authentication with IAM or OAuth helps make sure only authorized callers can invoke the hosted agent.

entities.name: BatchEvaluation
entities.overview:
A batch evaluation is an asynchronous job that scores many recorded agent sessions in a single run. It reads agent telemetry from Amazon CloudWatch Logs, or reuses sessions already sampled by an online evaluation configuration. It then applies a chosen set of evaluators to each session it discovers.

The service handles session discovery, span collection, and scoring, so teams do not need to build their own evaluation pipelines. Filters can narrow the scope to a time window, specific sessions, or specific traces. Optional ground truth, such as expected responses, assertions, and tool-call sequences, supports reference-based scoring.

Results include aggregate scores for each evaluator and counts of evaluated, failed, and skipped sessions. Insight evaluators can also group failures across sessions and suggest likely root causes and fixes. Per-session scores and explanations are written to CloudWatch Logs and published as metrics. Evaluation data can optionally be encrypted with a customer managed key. Teams use batch evaluations to set baselines, compare agent changes, and run regression tests.

entities.name: BrowserProfile
entities.overview:
A browser profile stores persistent browser state, such as cookies and local storage, captured from an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser session. You can load the saved state into later browser sessions so they start where an earlier session left off.

Browser profiles help AI agents stay signed in to websites across sessions, reducing repeated sign-in, single sign-on, and multi-factor prompts. They also help preserve preferences, shopping carts, and context for workflows that span several sessions.

Saving a session to a profile replaces the previously stored state, and only sessions started afterward use the update. Because profiles can hold authentication cookies, access is controlled through IAM policies scoped to profile resources.

entities.name: BrowserSession
entities.overview:
A browser session is an isolated, managed Chromium browser that an AI agent uses to navigate websites, fill in forms, and extract information. Each session runs in its own dedicated sandbox with separate compute, memory, and file system, and is torn down when it ends.

Agents control the session through an encrypted automation connection and can also perform operating system level mouse, keyboard, and screenshot actions. A live view lets people watch the session in real time and take over control when needed. Automation can be paused so a person can enter sign-in details the agent should not see.

Each session starts from a browser configuration that sets network access, recording, and baseline security settings. Per-session options include proxy routing, trusted root certificates, extensions, enterprise browser policies, saved profiles, and mounted file systems. Sessions end when stopped or when their configured time limit expires.

entities.name: CapacityProvider
entities.overview:
A capacity provider defines the Amazon EC2 infrastructure that hosts Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents on the Instances compute type. It specifies the operating system, allowed instance types, VPC placement, storage volumes, lifecycle limits, and the IAM role Amazon Bedrock AgentCore uses to manage instances.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore uses the capacity provider as a reusable template. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore launches managed EC2 instances from it in your own account when associated agent runtimes are invoked. Each session maps to one instance, and multiple agents can share a session to collaborate on a common filesystem.

This model is designed for long-running, stateful, or GPU-accelerated agent workloads. Persistent volumes keep data across session stops until the session is deleted. Deleting a session releases its instance, network interface, and persistent storage. Because instances run in your account and VPC, your existing account controls, network rules, and encryption settings help govern them.

entities.name: CodeInterpreter
entities.overview:
A code interpreter gives AI agents a managed, sandboxed environment for writing and running code. Agents use it to perform precise calculations, analyze structured data, process files, and create visualizations that reasoning alone cannot reliably produce.

It supports Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript with common data science libraries preinstalled. Agents can also run shell commands, manage files within a session, and work with larger datasets in Amazon S3 or mounted file systems.

Each session runs in its own isolated environment that is designed to be discarded when the session ends. You can tailor network access, permissions, file storage, and trusted certificate authorities to match your security and data requirements.

entities.name: CodeInterpreterSession
entities.overview:
A code interpreter session is an isolated, short-lived sandbox where an AI agent writes and runs code. Each session starts from a code interpreter and inherits its network access and permission settings.

Within a session, agents can run Python, JavaScript, or TypeScript code, execute shell commands, and read or write files. Variables, intermediate results, and files persist across executions until the session ends, which helps with multi-step analysis and computation.

Each session runs in its own dedicated environment, which is designed to keep one session's data separate from another's. Sessions end automatically after a configurable timeout or when you stop them, and their temporary data is then cleaned up. You can add trusted private certificate authorities and mount your own shared file systems to reach internal services and larger datasets.

entities.name: Evaluator
entities.overview:
An evaluator scores the quality of an AI agent's behavior using the telemetry the agent emits. It examines complete conversations, individual request-and-response turns, or single tool calls. It returns a score, a label, and a written explanation.

Ready-made evaluators cover common criteria such as helpfulness, correctness, goal completion, tool selection, and harmful content. Managed metrics from popular open-source evaluation libraries are also available without hosting them yourself. For domain-specific needs, you can define a custom evaluator that uses a judge model with your own instructions and rating scale. A custom evaluator can instead run your own AWS Lambda function for deterministic checks, such as format validation or business rules.

Evaluators help teams test agents during development, gate deployments in CI/CD pipelines, and monitor production quality over time. They can score selected interactions on demand, batches of recorded sessions, or a sample of live traffic.

entities.name: Event
entities.overview:
An event is a single, timestamped record of an interaction stored in the short-term memory of an AgentCore Memory resource. Agents use events to capture conversation turns, tool results, activity data, and binary content such as documents or saved agent state.

Events are organized by actor and session. This lets an agent reload a conversation exactly as it happened, continue it after a restart, or branch from an earlier message to explore an alternative path. Optional metadata helps applications filter and find relevant events without scanning whole sessions.

Events can also feed long-term memory. Configured strategies extract preferences, facts, and summaries from them, unless an event is marked to skip extraction. Events are immutable, kept for the retention period set on the parent memory, and can be permanently deleted on demand.

entities.name: Harness
entities.overview:
An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness is a managed agent loop that turns a declarative agent definition into a running agent. You declare the model, instructions, tools, skills, memory, and execution limits. The service then handles orchestration, tool execution, context management, and streamed responses.

Each session runs in an isolated microVM with its own filesystem and shell, so the agent can write and run code. Conversation history and long-term knowledge can persist across sessions through attached memory. Agents can use models from Amazon Bedrock or third-party providers and switch providers mid-session without losing context.

Tools connect through gateways, remote MCP servers, a managed browser, a code interpreter, or client-side functions for human approval steps. Defaults set on the harness can be overridden for a single invocation, which helps teams experiment quickly. Each configuration change is captured as an immutable version, and endpoints help teams promote or roll back versions in a controlled way. Agent actions are traced automatically to support monitoring and troubleshooting.

entities.name: Memory
entities.overview:
An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory is a fully managed store that gives AI agents persistent context across interactions. It keeps raw conversation history so an agent can resume a session without users repeating themselves. It can also distill conversations into durable insights, such as user preferences, facts, and summaries, for reuse in later sessions.

Configurable extraction strategies determine which information is retained and how it is organized. Hierarchical namespaces scope stored insights by user, session, or custom dimensions such as tenant or team. Agents retrieve the most relevant insights through semantic search to personalize their responses.

A memory helps teams avoid building and operating their own conversation storage and retrieval infrastructure. Data is encrypted at rest, optionally with a customer managed key, and retention periods can be tuned to governance needs.

entities.name: MemoryRecord
entities.overview:
A memory record is a structured unit of long-term knowledge that an AgentCore Memory keeps on behalf of an AI agent. Each record captures a distilled insight, such as a user preference, fact, or conversation summary, that the agent can recall in later sessions.

Records are produced automatically when memory strategies extract and consolidate information from conversations. They can also be written, updated, or removed directly by your own processing pipelines. Each record holds text content, timestamps, optional structured metadata, and a namespace that places it in a hierarchy, such as per user.

Agents can fetch a specific record, browse records within a namespace hierarchy, or run a semantic search ranked by relevance to a query. Namespaces and metadata filters help scope results to the right user or tenant. An optional time-to-live helps retire records after a retention period you choose.

entities.name: PaymentInstrument
entities.overview:
A payment instrument represents an end user's embedded crypto wallet that an AI agent uses to pay for APIs, tools, and web content. Each instrument is tied to one end user and one blockchain network, such as Ethereum-compatible chains or Solana. It links the wallet to the user's identity at the wallet provider, such as an email address, phone number, or social sign-in.

A new wallet starts with no funds. The end user funds it and grants the agent signing permission through the wallet provider's portal. The user can revoke that permission at any time. Private keys remain with the wallet provider rather than with the agent or the developer.

When an agent hits a paid resource, the service signs the payment from the instrument within a time-bound session that can cap spending. This helps agents transact on a user's behalf while spending stays within limits that the application sets. Developers can also check an instrument's balance and retire instruments they no longer need.

entities.name: PaymentSession
entities.overview:
A payment session is a time-bounded spending context for an AI agent acting on behalf of one end user. Each session belongs to a payment manager and carries an expiry time and an optional maximum spend amount. It also tracks how much of that budget remains as the agent pays for APIs, tools, and content.

Before signing any payment, the service checks the request against the session's remaining budget and expiry. Requests are denied once the session expires or its budget is exhausted. If signing fails after part of the budget is reserved, that amount returns to the available balance.

Because the service enforces these limits outside the agent's model, they help contain runaway, repeated, or manipulated spending. In the recommended pattern, trusted application code creates the session and passes only its reference to the agent.

entities.name: Recommendation
entities.overview:
A recommendation analyzes an agent's recorded session traces and proposes an improved system prompt or clearer tool descriptions. It helps teams move from manual trace review and prompt rewriting to evidence-based configuration changes.

For system prompts, you pick an evaluator as the target signal, and the service identifies failure patterns that lower that score. For tool descriptions, it looks for ambiguity that leads the agent to choose the wrong tool. Each result includes an explanation of the proposed changes.

Traces can come from Amazon CloudWatch Logs, earlier evaluation results, or spans supplied directly. The current configuration can be passed as text or read from a versioned configuration bundle. Bundle-based runs write the optimized output back as a new version. Suggestions are model-generated and are designed to be reviewed and validated, for example with A/B testing, before use.

entities.name: Registry
entities.overview:
A registry is a governed catalog for publishing and discovering agentic resources across an organization. Records describe agents, tools, MCP servers, and skills, capturing what each resource does and how to reach it.

Administrators configure each registry with its own inbound authorization, using either AWS IAM credentials or JSON Web Tokens from a corporate identity provider. An approval setting determines whether submitted records need curator review before they become discoverable. Registry content is encrypted at rest, with an option to use a customer managed key.

Consumers, including people and AI agents, search a registry with natural language or keyword queries and can narrow results with metadata filters. Only approved records are returned, which helps teams reuse vetted tools instead of rebuilding them.

entities.name: ResourceApiKey
entities.overview:
A resource API key is the stored secret an agent uses to authenticate to external services that rely on key-based access. AgentCore Identity keeps the key in encrypted, access-controlled storage and releases it to authorized agent workloads at runtime.

Central storage helps you avoid embedding secrets in agent code, prompts, or configuration files. Retrieval requires both IAM permission and proof of the calling workload's identity. This lets you limit each key to the specific agents that need it.

You can let the service manage the backing secret or reference your own secret in AWS Secrets Manager. When a key is rotated or replaced, agents receive the current value on their next retrieval.

entities.name: ResourceOauth2Token
entities.overview:
A resource OAuth2 token is an OAuth 2.0 access token that lets an agent call an external API, tool, or MCP server. AgentCore Identity brokers the OAuth flow with the configured authorization server and keeps the resulting tokens in its token vault. This design helps keep client secrets and long-term credentials out of agent code.

A token can represent the agent itself for machine-to-machine access. It can also represent a consenting end user through an authorization code flow, or an authenticated user through on-behalf-of token exchange. Stored user tokens are bound to one agent identity and one end user. This helps prevent reuse of credentials across users or agents.

For user-delegated access, the service returns a short-lived authorization link and tracks the consent session. Your application then confirms that the user who granted consent is the same user who started the request. After this confirmation, the service exchanges the authorization code and stores the resulting token. When the provider issues refresh tokens, expired access tokens are renewed automatically, which helps reduce repeated consent prompts.

entities.name: ResourcePaymentToken
entities.overview:
A resource payment token is a vendor-specific authentication credential that AgentCore Identity generates on demand for agent payment workflows. It is derived from developer credentials held in a payment credential provider, so agent code does not need to store those keys.

Each token is produced for a specific provider request, such as a call to Coinbase Developer Platform or Stripe Privy. Depending on the provider, it can carry bearer credentials, wallet authorization for signing operations, or a time-limited request signature.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments uses these tokens to instruct wallet providers to perform wallet operations, such as signing transactions. Access is tied to the caller's workload identity and IAM permissions, which helps limit which agents can reach wallet resources.

entities.name: WorkloadAccessToken
entities.overview:
A workload access token is a short-lived, AWS-signed credential that represents an agent's workload identity within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. When an agent acts for an end user, the token also carries that user's identity, binding the two together.

Agents present the token to AgentCore Identity to retrieve OAuth tokens, API keys, and other credentials held in the token vault. Because retrieval is scoped to the agent and user pair, the token helps keep one user's stored credentials separate from another's.

Tokens can be issued for an agent working on its own or on behalf of a user. User identity comes from a verified identity provider token or an application-supplied identifier. AgentCore Runtime and Gateway obtain these tokens and pass them to agents automatically, and self-hosted agents can request them directly.

mitigations.statement: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls from your VPCs can target resources in another account. Restricting those calls to resources in your organization enforces the resource perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls from your VPCs can be made by identities outside your organization. Restricting those calls to principals in your organization enforces the identity perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test's execution role should be assumed only by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: The `$.roleArn` request parameter sets or replaces your A/B test's IAM execution role, and that role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: When you call `CreateABTest`, you can tag the A/B test through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map of up to 50 tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each A/B test supports.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime resources

mitigationContext.context: Resource-based policies on an agent runtime and its endpoint in another account can grant your principals access to that runtime. That access includes invoking the hosted agent or tool, running commands in runtime sessions, and stopping those sessions. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime should be configured to send application and trace logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore produces application logs for each invocation of your agent runtime, recording the operation, request ID, session ID, trace IDs and request payload, and trace spans for each `InvokeAgentRuntime` call, recording the agent runtime, endpoint, session ID, latency and error type. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: When you call `StartBatchEvaluation`, the `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter specifies the key that encrypts your batch evaluation's stored artifacts. Using a customer managed key instead of the default AWS owned key gives you full control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: When you start a batch evaluation with `StartBatchEvaluation`, you tag it through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map of up to 50 tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each batch evaluation supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter should be configured to send application and trace logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore produces application logs for each `InvokeCodeInterpreter` call to your code interpreter, recording its session identifier and request and response payloads, and trace spans for each `StartCodeInterpreterSession`, `InvokeCodeInterpreter` and `StopCodeInterpreterSession` call, recording the code interpreter, tool session ID, latency and error type. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only events in trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memories

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in another account can grant your principals access to write, read, list and delete that memory's events. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in another account can grant your principals data plane access to that memory. Each `IngestData`, `ListActors`, `ListSessions`, `ListMemoryExtractionJobs`, and `StartMemoryExtractionJob` request names the memory it targets. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory should be configured to send application and trace logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore produces application logs that record your memory's deletion and its long-term memory extraction and consolidation workflows with actor and session identifiers, and trace spans that record `CreateEvent`, `GetEvent`, `ListEvents`, `DeleteEvent`, `RetrieveMemoryRecords` and `ListMemoryRecords` calls with memory, session, event, actor or namespace identifiers. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only records in trusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memories

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in another account can grant your principals access to its long-term memory records. That access can include calls that write, update, delete, read, list, or semantically search those records. The resource perimeter helps restrict your identities to resources your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: When you start a recommendation, the `$.kmsKeyArn` request parameter specifies an AWS KMS customer managed key that encrypts the recommendation's configuration and result. Using a customer managed key for this encryption gives you control over the key's lifecycle and permissions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a recommendation when you call `StartRecommendation`, through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map of up to 50 tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each recommendation supports.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service API calls

threatContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is reachable from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). An IAM principal from outside your organization can use that network path to make Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls with its own credentials. That access enables transfer of data from your VPC to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memories, agent runtimes, and code interpreters in an AWS account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore data plane API calls from your VPCs can target agent runtimes, memories, and other Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources in another account. With permissions on such a resource, an IAM principal on your network can send your data to an agent runtime or write it into a memory as events and records.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test
threats.threatAction: can configure the A/B test without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test can omit the required tags, because `$.tags{key}` is optional on `CreateABTest`. An A/B test left without those tags still splits live traffic between variants and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test's IAM execution role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my execution role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test designates an IAM execution role through `$.roleArn`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted agent runtime, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: An agent runtime in an account outside your organization can grant your principals access through resource-based policies on both the runtime and its endpoint. Your principals can then call `InvokeAgentRuntime` to send data in `$.payload`, or call `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand` to run shell commands in the runtime's session container. Both calls exchange data with an environment that the runtime's owner controls, outside your governance.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime
threats.threatAction: can interact with the agent runtime without a record of their activities being persisted by application and trace log delivery

threatContext.context: When application and trace log delivery are not configured on your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime, no per-invocation application log records or `InvokeAgentRuntime` spans are written by application and trace log delivery. An IAM principal with permissions to use the agent runtime can send request payloads to the agent runtime by invoking it, leaving no record of those request payloads or the calls that sent them persisted by application and trace log delivery.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime
threats.threatAction: can disable application and trace log delivery for the agent runtime

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime can use CloudWatch Logs permissions to call `DeleteDelivery`, then `DeleteDeliverySource`. Removing a delivery stops the log type it carries, the opt-in per-invocation application log records or the `InvokeAgentRuntime` spans, from reaching CloudWatch Logs while your agent runtime keeps serving `InvokeAgentRuntime` and `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand` calls.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the batch evaluation's stored artifacts, such as per-session ground truth, evaluation results, and insight results, with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to start a batch evaluation chooses the KMS key that encrypts the batch evaluation's stored artifacts by setting `$.kmsKeyArn`. If that key material sits outside your control, its holder can later revoke or delete it and leave those artifacts unreadable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation
threats.threatAction: can configure the batch evaluation without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation can omit the required tags, because `$.tags{key}` on `StartBatchEvaluation` is optional. A batch evaluation left without those tags still holds its evaluation results and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation
threats.threatAction: can encrypt its output artifacts with an AWS owned KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle and to audit key usage through CloudTrail

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to create your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation chooses whether the AWS owned key protects its output artifacts at rest. You cannot govern that key's policy or lifecycle, and the service's use of it produces no CloudTrail events in your account.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read evaluation and insight results from an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext evaluation and insight results in the batch evaluation

threatContext.context: Without a customer managed key, your batch evaluation's output artifacts, including evaluation and insight results, are encrypted under an AWS owned key that you cannot manage or audit. An IAM principal holding the permission to call `GetBatchEvaluation` can read those results in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read evaluation results and insight results from an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation that has been encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key
threats.threatAction: can read evaluation results and insight results in the batch evaluation

threatContext.context: By default, your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluation's evaluation results and insight results are encrypted at rest with an AWS owned key. That key type gives you no key policy to govern, no audit record of key use, and no control over the key lifecycle, so an IAM principal granted broader permissions than intended can retrieve them in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter
threats.threatAction: can interact with the code interpreter without a record of their activities being persisted by application and trace log delivery to CloudWatch Logs

threatContext.context: When application and trace log delivery are not configured on your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter, no application logs or spans are written by application and trace log delivery to CloudWatch Logs. An IAM principal with permissions to use the code interpreter can run code, run shell commands, and access files, leaving no record of the code, commands, or file contents, or of the calls that ran them, persisted by application and trace log delivery.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter
threats.threatAction: can disable application and trace log delivery for the code interpreter

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter can use CloudWatch Logs permissions to delete its log delivery with `DeleteDelivery` or overwrite its delivery source with `PutDeliverySource`. Either change stops the opt-in application logs or spans the affected delivery carries from reaching CloudWatch Logs while code execution, shell commands, and file operations in its sessions continue without those records.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory
threats.threatAction: can interact with events in the untrusted memory, including sending data to them or receiving data from them

threatContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in an account outside your organization can grant your principals access through its resource-based policy. Your principals with IAM permissions on that memory can then call `CreateEvent` to write conversation text, JSON data, or binary content into storage that account controls. If that policy also grants read access, they can call `GetEvent` to retrieve events from that memory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted memory, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in an account outside your organization can grant your principals access through its resource-based policy. Your principals with IAM permissions on that memory can then call `IngestData` to send it conversational text in `$.source.inline.payload[*].conversational.content.text` or JSON in `$.source.inline.payload[*].json.content`.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory
threats.threatAction: can interact with the memory without a record of their activities being persisted by application and trace log delivery

threatContext.context: When application and trace log delivery are not configured on your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, no application logs or spans are written by log delivery. An IAM principal with permissions to use the memory can interact with it, leaving no record of the long-term memory extraction and consolidation those interactions trigger, or of the calls themselves, persisted by log delivery.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory
threats.threatAction: can disable application and trace log delivery for the memory

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory can call `DeleteDelivery` with the `$.id` of a log delivery for the memory, then call `DeleteDeliverySource` with the delivery source's `$.name`. That change stops the memory's opt-in application logs or spans, whichever delivery it removes, from reaching CloudWatch Logs.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory
threats.threatAction: can interact with records in the untrusted memory, including sending data to them or receiving data from them

threatContext.context: An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory in an account outside your organization can grant your principals access through a resource-based policy. Your principals whose own permissions also cover that memory can then write your data into its records by calling `BatchCreateMemoryRecords` or `BatchUpdateMemoryRecords`. They can also read record content from that memory by calling `GetMemoryRecord` or `RetrieveMemoryRecords`.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the recommendation's input data and AI-generated results with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to start a recommendation chooses the KMS key that encrypts your recommendation data by setting `$.kmsKeyArn`. If that key material sits outside your control, its holder can later revoke or delete it and leave that recommendation data unreadable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation
threats.threatAction: can configure the recommendation without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation can omit the required tags, because `$.tags{key}` on `StartRecommendation` is optional. A recommendation left without those tags still persists until you delete it and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation
threats.threatAction: can encrypt its configuration and result with an AWS owned KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle and to audit key usage through CloudTrail

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to create your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation chooses whether the AWS owned key protects its configuration and result at rest. You cannot govern that key's policy or lifecycle, and the service's use of it produces no CloudTrail events in your account.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read configuration and result data from an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext configuration and result data in the recommendation

threatContext.context: Without a customer managed key, your recommendation's configuration and result, including trace content, are encrypted under an AWS owned key that you cannot restrict, audit or disable. An IAM principal holding the permission to call `GetRecommendation` can read the configuration and result in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read system prompts, tool descriptions, and trace-derived optimization results from an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation that has been encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key
threats.threatAction: can read system prompts, tool descriptions, and trace-derived optimization results in the recommendation

threatContext.context: By default, your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore recommendation's system prompts, tool descriptions, and trace-derived optimization results are encrypted at rest with an AWS owned key. That key type gives you no key policy to govern, no audit record of key use, and no control over the key lifecycle, so an IAM principal granted broader permissions than intended can retrieve them in plaintext.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends using your VPC endpoint policy to govern Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls made through the endpoint with the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key. As a result, calls to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources outside your organization are restricted, while AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) remain exempt.

To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Use `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` to allow AWS services to use their service principals to send requests from your network. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends recording Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls made through your VPC endpoints, which are logged with an `eventSource` of `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com`. Each event shows the account and principal that made the call, in `userIdentity`, and which operation they called. A call that violates your VPC endpoint policy carries an `errorCode` of `VpceAccessDenied`, helping you detect attempts to reach untrusted resources.

These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.roleArn`, your A/B test's execution role, then evaluating `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`, that role's trust policy, with IAM Access Analyzer. Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy that restricts assumption of your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test's execution role, `$.roleArn`, to the `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` service principal with the `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` condition keys. These conditions help prevent Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from assuming the role on behalf of A/B tests outside the sources you specify.

Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test's execution role, `$.roleArn`.

To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.tags{key}` on each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A/B test listed through `$.abTests[*].abTestArn` and flagging any that omit your required owner and purpose tag keys. Surfacing those resources helps you attribute each A/B test to an accountable owner and the business function it supports.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls. As a result, your identities are restricted from accessing agent runtimes outside your organization, except through OAuth bearer-token calls made without IAM credentials.

To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation guidance recommends recording the CloudWatch Logs operations that can disable or weaken the vended logs delivery for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime. Recording calls such as `DeleteDelivery`, `DeleteDeliverySource`, and `PutRetentionPolicy`, together with the calling identity, helps you detect and attribute those changes.

This implementation guidance recommends flagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime with no vended logs delivery to CloudWatch Logs, read from `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationType`, the delivery's destination type. Surfacing that gap helps you detect agent runtime invocation activity that is not being recorded for review.

This implementation guidance recommends recording `GetBatchEvaluation` calls against your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore batch evaluations, along with the identity that made each call. Recording those calls helps you detect and investigate authorized-but-unexpected access to the data protected by your customer managed key.

Enforcing a customer managed key governs which key protects the data. It does not record which permitted principals read that data. The data events this guide monitors record those reads. CloudTrail does not log data events by default, and they are high volume. To scope log volume and cost, add advanced event selectors to the trail or event data store. Filter `resources.ARN` to the governed resources, using `Equals` for exact ARNs or `StartsWith` for a naming prefix. Filter `eventName` to the operations this guide monitors. A `readOnly` filter selects by CloudTrail's read or write classification, not by this guide's operation set, so do not rely on it alone. A trail or event data store accepts at most 500 values across all advanced event selector conditions.
